questions.question: A sparkler's spark (≈2000 °C) touching skin does less damage than a cup of 90 °C tea. Resolve with the heat-temperature distinction.
questions.solution: Temperature measures the AVERAGE kinetic energy of particles; heat is ENERGY TRANSFERRED, which depends on mass and contact time. A spark has enormous temperature but negligible mass — tiny total energy. The tea has lower temperature but much more thermal energy to deliver. Damage tracks energy delivered, not temperature alone.

questions.concept: Thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law
questions.question: Why does a thermometer 'measure' the temperature of your body — what principle makes that possible?
questions.solution: Contact lets heat flow between thermometer and body until they reach THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM (same temperature). The zeroth law says bodies in equilibrium with a third body are in equilibrium with each other — so the thermometer, calibrated, reports the body's temperature. Measurement by equilibrium is the principle.

questions.question: Why does the same burner heat 1 kg of water much more slowly than 1 kg of iron? Quantify the idea with specific heat.
questions.solution: Q = mcΔT: for the same heat input, ΔT = Q/mc. Water's specific heat (4186 J/kg·K) is ~10× iron's (~450), so water's temperature rises ~10× less. Water's high c is why it is used as a coolant and why coastal climates are mild.

questions.concept: Latent heat — energy without temperature change
questions.question: Melting ice stays at 0 °C while absorbing heat. Where does that energy go?
questions.solution: Into LATENT heat — breaking the intermolecular bonds of the solid structure, increasing potential energy of the molecules while their average KE (temperature) stays constant. The temperature plateau during phase change is the signature of latent heat; the energy reappears as heat when the substance freezes.

questions.question: Hot metal dropped into cold water: why is 'heat lost by metal = heat gained by water' valid, and what assumption hides inside it?
questions.solution: Energy conservation: in an isolated container, no heat escapes, so the transfers must balance — m₁c₁ΔT₁ = m₂c₂ΔT₂. Hidden assumption: NO heat leaks to the surroundings and none is lost to the calorimeter itself unless its heat capacity is included. Ignoring the container is the classic experimental error.

questions.concept: Why water has a high boiling point
questions.question: Water (Mr 18) boils at 100 °C while methane (Mr 16) boils at −161 °C. Why is such a light molecule so hard to boil apart?
questions.solution: Boiling requires breaking intermolecular forces, and water's strong HYDROGEN BONDS hold its molecules together far more than the weak van der Waals forces of methane. Light but strongly associating molecules can have high boiling points; mass is only one factor. H-bond networks are the anomaly that lifts water far above its molecular-mass prediction.

questions.concept: Why the mixture warms then cools
questions.question: Mixing equal masses of 80 °C water and 20 °C water gives 50 °C. Why is the result exactly the average rather than something else?
questions.solution: Heat lost by the hot = heat gained by the cold: mc(80−T) = mc(T−20). With equal mass and same c, (80−T) = (T−20) → T = 50 °C exactly. The equality-of-transfers equation is the whole physics; the average falls out because both sides share mc. Different masses or capacities would shift the balance point.

questions.concept: Why steam burns worse than boiling water
questions.question: A burn from 100 °C steam is often worse than one from 100 °C water. Where does the extra energy come from?
questions.solution: On contact, steam first CONDENSES, releasing its latent heat (2260 kJ/kg) onto the skin — on top of the sensible heat it delivers as 100 °C water cooling. Condensation pumps far more energy in per gram than simple cooling. Same temperature, but steam carries the hidden phase-change payload.
